variants.title: Build the gateway decision
variants.context: The request body is untrusted. The gateway builds its decision from trusted context: bind identity, normalize intent into a product-level envelope, filter routes by hard constraints, then rank only eligible routes, fetching the chosen adapter's credential just in time and preserving native response semantics.
variants.prompt: An application submits a summarization request through the gateway. Put the gateway's decision steps in order.

items.text: Build a product-level envelope with task type, input blocks, required capabilities, output limit, deadline, and cancellation signal.
Reject candidate routes that violate capability, context, tenant, safety, residency, health, quota, budget, or deadline constraints.
Score the remaining eligible routes for quality, latency, and cost under the versioned policy.
Obtain the chosen adapter's credential just in time, invoke it, and preserve the native response semantics.
Verify the caller and derive tenant, plan, allowed data classes, regions, and policy version from trusted identity data.

variants.hint: Hard rules run before any score is computed.
variants.explanation: Bind, normalize, filter, rank, invoke: eligibility is deterministic and happens before optimization so a cheap route can never override a hard rule.

variants.title: Build the gateway decision
variants.context: The request body is untrusted. The gateway builds its decision from trusted context: bind identity, normalize intent into a product-level envelope, filter routes by hard constraints, then rank only eligible routes, fetching the chosen adapter's credential just in time and preserving native response semantics.
variants.prompt: A client sends its own tenant header and a plan tier claiming a larger budget. Put the gateway's steps in order.

items.text: Invoke the adapter and attribute usage to the authenticated tenant.
Rank the eligible routes and resolve the credential for the winner after the policy decision.
Filter routes against the trusted tenant's residency, safety, quota, and budget constraints.
Ignore the client's tenant and plan claims and bind tenant and budget from the authenticated identity.
Normalize the requested task, capabilities, output limit, and deadline into the envelope.

variants.hint: Who is allowed to say which tenant this is?
variants.explanation: A client may suggest a task or deadline, but tenant, residency, plan, and budget come from trusted identity.

variants.title: Build the gateway decision
variants.context: The request body is untrusted. The gateway builds its decision from trusted context: bind identity, normalize intent into a product-level envelope, filter routes by hard constraints, then rank only eligible routes, fetching the chosen adapter's credential just in time and preserving native response semantics.
variants.prompt: A request carries regulated data that may only be processed in one region. Put the gateway's steps in order.

items.text: Rank whatever is left, and deny the request if no compliant route remains.
Invoke the compliant adapter and record the region actually served.
Bind identity and attach the tenant's allowed data classes and regions.
Filter out every route whose region, network path, or safety profile is not compliant.
Normalize intent and classify the data so the residency requirement is part of the envelope.

variants.hint: Residency is a constraint, not a ranking hint.
variants.explanation: Safety and data residency are route constraints applied before ranking; a request with no compliant route is denied, not routed to the cheapest option.

variants.title: Cancel a stream end to end
variants.context: Streaming cancellation is an end-to-end signal: stop forwarding events, abort the gateway task, ask the adapter to cancel the native stream, record whether the provider confirmed cancellation and any final usage, and keep the canceled result out of the response cache. Unconfirmed cancellation keeps the budget reservation until usage is reconciled.
variants.prompt: A browser closes its tab in the middle of a streamed answer. Put the gateway's cancellation steps in order.

items.text: Prevent the canceled partial result from entering the response cache.
Ask the active adapter to cancel or close the native provider stream.
Record whether the provider confirmed cancellation and any final usage.
Abort the gateway task that owns the request.
Stop forwarding stream events to the client.

variants.hint: Work inward from the client toward the provider, then account.
variants.explanation: Cancellation flows from client to gateway to adapter, then the outcome is recorded and the partial result is kept out of caches.

variants.title: Cancel a stream end to end
variants.context: Streaming cancellation is an end-to-end signal: stop forwarding events, abort the gateway task, ask the adapter to cancel the native stream, record whether the provider confirmed cancellation and any final usage, and keep the canceled result out of the response cache. Unconfirmed cancellation keeps the budget reservation until usage is reconciled.
variants.prompt: The product's deadline expires while the provider is still streaming. Put the cancellation steps in order.

items.text: Keep the incomplete output out of the response cache.
Send a cancel or close to the adapter's native stream.
Abort the gateway task and mark the request as deadline-exceeded.
Record the provider's confirmation and the tokens it reports as billed.
Stop delivering further events to the application.

variants.hint: The deadline triggers the same path as a disconnect.
variants.explanation: Deadline expiry is a cancellation like any other; the gateway stops, aborts, cancels natively, records usage, and refuses to cache the partial result.

variants.title: Cancel a stream end to end
variants.context: Streaming cancellation is an end-to-end signal: stop forwarding events, abort the gateway task, ask the adapter to cancel the native stream, record whether the provider confirmed cancellation and any final usage, and keep the canceled result out of the response cache. Unconfirmed cancellation keeps the budget reservation until usage is reconciled.
variants.prompt: A cancellation is sent, but the provider's API never confirms whether generation stopped. Put the steps in order, ending with how the budget is handled.

items.text: Block the result from the response cache and expose the unknown outcome in telemetry.
Keep the budget reservation until authoritative usage is reconciled.
Ask the adapter to cancel the native stream.
Mark the outcome unknown because the provider did not confirm cancellation.
Stop forwarding events and abort the gateway task.

variants.hint: A timeout or silence does not prove the provider did no work.
variants.explanation: When cancellation is unconfirmed, the gateway treats the work as possibly billed: unknown outcome, nothing cached, reservation held until usage arrives.

variants.title: Reserve the budget
variants.context: Reserve budget before admission against the maximum permitted output, not an optimistic average, and reconcile every attempt afterward. Attempt amplification is total provider attempts divided by client requests, and only eligible routes may be ranked.
variants.prompt: A route charges $1.00 per million input tokens and $4.00 per million output tokens. Requests average 4,000 input tokens; output averages 500 tokens but the permitted maximum is 1,000. How many dollars should the gateway reserve per 1,000 requests?
variants.hint: Which output figure does a reservation use?
variants.explanation: Input 4,000 / 1M x $1 = $0.004 and output 1,000 / 1M x $4 = $0.004, so $0.008 per request or $8 per 1,000.

mistakes.feedback: Reserve against the maximum permitted output of 1,000 tokens, not the 500-token average.
Add the output reservation; input is only half the estimate.

variants.title: Reserve the budget
variants.context: Reserve budget before admission against the maximum permitted output, not an optimistic average, and reconcile every attempt afterward. Attempt amplification is total provider attempts divided by client requests, and only eligible routes may be ranked.
variants.prompt: In one hour, 1,000 client requests produced 1,000 primary attempts, 150 retries, and 50 fallback attempts. What is the attempt amplification, in attempts per client request?
variants.hint: Every provider attempt counts, whatever its role.
variants.explanation: (1,000 + 150 + 50) / 1,000 = 1.2 attempts per request; the gateway exposes this so retry storms are visible.

mistakes.feedback: Fallback attempts are billable provider attempts too.
Charging only the winning attempt hides retries and fallbacks from the budget.

variants.title: Reserve the budget
variants.context: Reserve budget before admission against the maximum permitted output, not an optimistic average, and reconcile every attempt afterward. Attempt amplification is total provider attempts divided by client requests, and only eligible routes may be ranked.
variants.prompt: Six candidate routes exist. Two fail the tenant's residency rule, one cannot fit the request's context length, and one has an open circuit breaker. How many routes may the ranking policy score?
variants.explanation: Residency, context, and health are hard constraints, leaving 6 - 2 - 1 - 1 = 2 eligible routes for ranking.

mistakes.feedback: Ranking scores only eligible candidates; filter first.
An open circuit is a health constraint, so that route is ineligible too.

variants.title: Contain the failure
variants.context: Contain failure by classification: retry only transient failures inside the deadline and retry budget, charging every attempt; scope circuit breakers to the failing route; and require fallbacks to pass the same eligibility filter and a measured quality floor.
variants.prompt: A provider call exceeds the gateway's timeout with 40% of the request deadline remaining. What should the gateway do?
options: Retry only if the failure classifies as transient and the retry budget allows, charging both attempts.
Never retry a timeout; return an error to the client immediately every time.
Retry immediately at full depth, since a timeout proves the provider did no work.
optionFeedback: Retries follow classification, deadline, and budget, and every attempt is charged to the tenant.
Some timeouts are transient, and a bounded retry inside the deadline is legitimate.
A timeout only means completion was not observed; a retry can be a second billable generation.
variants.hint: What does a timeout actually prove?
variants.explanation: Retry by classified failure, within the original deadline and retry budget, with every attempt charged.

variants.title: Contain the failure
variants.context: Contain failure by classification: retry only transient failures inside the deadline and retry budget, charging every attempt; scope circuit breakers to the failing route; and require fallbacks to pass the same eligibility filter and a measured quality floor.
variants.prompt: One model deployment in one region starts returning errors while the provider's other models are healthy. How should the circuit breaker be keyed?
options: By provider, so all of its traffic fails over at once.
By provider, model or deployment, region, and operation.
No breaker; let per-request retries absorb the errors.
optionFeedback: A provider-wide circuit ejects healthy models and enlarges the blast radius.
A narrow circuit key ejects only the unhealthy route and keeps unrelated models serving.
Retries against a failing route amplify load and cost.
variants.hint: How small can the ejected surface be?
variants.explanation: Scope circuit breakers to the failing route; opening one circuit should not disable unrelated models.

variants.title: Contain the failure
variants.context: Contain failure by classification: retry only transient failures inside the deadline and retry budget, charging every attempt; scope circuit breakers to the failing route; and require fallbacks to pass the same eligibility filter and a measured quality floor.
variants.prompt: The primary route is ejected. A healthy, cheaper route exists in another region, but it lacks the output filtering the tenant's policy requires. Is it an eligible fallback?
options: Yes, availability is the priority during an outage.
Yes, if the gateway applies its own output checks afterward.
No, a fallback must keep the same or stricter region, safety, and quality contract.
optionFeedback: Availability does not suspend residency or safety policy.
Product-level checks add to native controls; they do not license leaving the allowed geography.
Fallback uses the same eligibility filter as the primary route and must meet the quality floor.
variants.hint: Does the fallback pass the same filter the primary passed?
variants.explanation: A fallback that leaves the allowed geography or loses required filtering is not eligible; returning text is not a fallback contract.

variants.title: Assign ownership by layer
variants.context: Four layers own different things: the application owns user intent and the experience, the gateway owns trusted policy and containment, the adapter owns translation to one provider API, and the provider owns execution under its own limits and billing.
variants.prompt: Match each layer to what it owns.

pairs.label: Application
pairs.detail: The user experience, conversation state, product deadline, and handling of a partial or canceled stream.

pairs.label: Gateway
pairs.detail: Trusted identity, tenant policy, quota, budget, route eligibility, release policy, and audit evidence.

pairs.label: Adapter
pairs.detail: Native request mapping, error classification, stream parsing, and usage normalization for one API.

pairs.label: Provider
pairs.detail: The served model, platform limits, native safety mechanisms, and billing semantics.

variants.hint: Trusted decisions sit in the middle; translation sits next to the API.
variants.explanation: The gateway coordinates policy across adapters; each adapter preserves one provider's exact semantics.

variants.prompt: Match each event in a request's life to the layer responsible for it.

pairs.label: Application
pairs.detail: Deciding what the user sees when a stream ends early.

pairs.label: Gateway
pairs.detail: Reserving budget and creating the request and attempt IDs.

pairs.label: Adapter
pairs.detail: Parsing a provider's native stream events and finish reasons.

pairs.label: Provider
pairs.detail: Executing the request under its documented regional behavior and limits.

variants.hint: Ask which contract the event belongs to: product, policy, API, or execution.
variants.explanation: Each level of the request has its own owner and its own identifiers and measurements.

variants.title: Assign ownership by layer
variants.context: Four layers own different things: the application owns user intent and the experience, the gateway owns trusted policy and containment, the adapter owns translation to one provider API, and the provider owns execution under its own limits and billing.
variants.prompt: Match each layer to its rule for credentials and identity.

pairs.label: Application
pairs.detail: Never selects a provider secret or claims its own tenant.

pairs.label: Gateway
pairs.detail: Resolves the credential only after policy has chosen a route, and attributes usage to the authenticated tenant.

pairs.label: Adapter
pairs.detail: Holds only the provider, project, model, and region permissions it needs.

pairs.label: Provider
pairs.detail: Bills the project whose credential was presented, under its own billing semantics.

variants.hint: Secret custody stays inside trusted infrastructure.
variants.explanation: Credentials are resolved just in time inside the gateway, scoped narrowly per adapter, and never handed to the application.
